notes.meaning: Joshua woke up early to lead Israel out of Shittim, their last campsite before the river. The people marched to the edge of the Jordan and camped there before crossing. Moving promptly showed Joshua's faith and his eagerness to do God's work without delay.

After three days of waiting by the river, Joshua's officers went through the camp to give fresh orders. The delay gave this large crowd of families and animals time to get ready, while looking at a flooded river they could not cross on their own.

The officers told the people to watch for the priests carrying the ark of the covenant and then follow it. The ark was a sacred gold-covered chest that represented God's throne and presence among them. Instead of soldiers or engineers leading the way, God himself was going out in front of his people.

The people were told to stay about half a mile behind the ark and not crowd around it. This large distance kept the holy ark visible to the whole traveling multitude so they would know where to go. It also taught the nation to approach the holy God with deep reverence and awe.

Joshua commanded the people to consecrate themselves, because God was going to perform great wonders among them the next day. Consecrating meant turning away from ordinary routines and washing themselves to focus entirely on the Lord. Preparing the heart in faith and repentance is fitting before God displays his mighty power.

Joshua directed the priests to lift the ark and walk ahead of the nation, and they obeyed. This changed the usual marching order, where the ark traveled in the middle of the tribes. Stepping out in front showed that the Lord was guiding and protecting his people through every unknown danger.

The Lord told Joshua that he would begin to honor him publicly in the eyes of all Israel that very day. By parting the Jordan through Joshua, God would prove to the people that he was with Joshua just as he had been with Moses. God establishes godly leaders so his people can trust and follow them.

God instructed Joshua to tell the priests carrying the ark to step directly into the water at the river's edge and halt there. They were not to wait safely on the dry bank for the river to disappear. Carrying the ark into the flowing water called for steady, active obedience before the miracle took place.

Joshua gathered the Israelites together so they could hear the message that came directly from God. He wanted their faith to rest on God's spoken promises before they witnessed the mighty deed itself. Listening carefully to God's word prepares his people to recognize his work.

Joshua told the people that this coming miracle would prove the living God was present among them. It gave them a sure pledge that he would drive out the seven pagan nations occupying Canaan. Unlike the lifeless idols of the land, Israel's God possesses the life and power to fulfill all his promises.

Joshua announced that the ark of the covenant, belonging to the Lord of all the earth, was going before them into the river. Calling God the Lord of all the earth reminded them that he is not a small, local deity of the hills or valleys. Because he rules over every river and nation, he has total power to clear a way for his people.

Joshua commanded the people to select twelve men, choosing one from each tribe of Israel. He did not tell them their assignment yet, but he kept them ready beside the leaders. This ensured every tribe would have an equal part in setting up the memorial that would soon follow.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Christian writers such as Gregory of Nyssa saw the twelve chosen men and their stones as pointing forward to the twelve apostles who would minister Christian baptism.

notes.meaning: Joshua revealed how the miracle would unfold: the moment the priests carrying the ark stepped into the river, the rushing current would be cut off. The waters flowing down from upstream would pile up in a heap, leaving an empty riverbed below. God's exact prediction proved that this wonder was entirely his doing and not a chance event.

The people packed up their tents and marched toward the Jordan, with the priests carrying the ark out ahead of them. Setting out while the river was still rushing past was an act of genuine faith. Both the priests and the people moved forward simply because they trusted God's word.

The river was overflowing its banks because the spring harvest coincided with heavy runoff from melting snow on the northern mountains. This dangerous flood made crossing humanly impossible, yet the priests stepped forward until their feet touched the water's edge. God chose the most difficult time of year so that his great power would be unmistakable.

As soon as the priests' feet touched the water, the river stopped flowing and piled up far upstream near the town of Adam, while the water below drained away into the Dead Sea. This left a wide stretch of dry riverbed right opposite the fortified city of Jericho. God completely opened the path right in front of the strongest enemy stronghold.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that natural mudslides near Adam have blocked the Jordan in later centuries, suggesting God may have used an earth collapse to dam the water.

notes.meaning: The priests carried the ark into the middle of the riverbed and stood firm on dry ground until the entire nation had safely crossed. The riverbed was completely dry, not muddy or slick, allowing hundreds of thousands of people to pass without trouble. God holds back life's overwhelming floods until all his people are safely across.

differ.view: Crossing the Jordan has long been viewed as a picture of the Christian passing through death into the rest of heaven.
The crossing pictures the believer dying with Christ and entering a life of spiritual warfare and faith, rather than heaven, because Canaan was full of battles.
The miracle of passing through the Jordan is seen as an Old Testament picture of baptism, where Christ leads his people through water into his kingdom.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early Church Fathers like Gregory and Augustine taught that the river rolling back foreshadows the grace of Christian baptism, which turns a believer back toward God.
